summary: A 1970 note with thoughts and reflections on RFC 54, which it updates. It is a discussion contribution from two authors.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 57 proposes ways to distinguish a protocol error from a host that has run out of resources. It also proposes a reset exchange so hosts can recover their connection state after a crash.

questions: what is the ovf command in rfc 57
subtitle: Proposals to distinguish NCP errors from resource overflow and recover after host crashes.

tldr.problem: RFC 54 reported resource exhaustion like a refused connection and did not define a recovery exchange for a host that crashed and restarted.
tldr.mechanism: The authors propose typed ERR codes, an OVF command for resource overflow, and RST/RSR commands for resetting connections and announcing that a host is alive.
tldr.outcome: The ideas were omitted from the official protocol proposal and offered for discussion and possible later inclusion.

today: RFC 57 is listed with status Unknown and updates RFC 54. The memo presents proposals for discussion, not a final protocol specification.

sections.title: Ideas Left Out of RFC 54
sections.content:
While writing RFC 54, the authors identified ideas that were either new to the working group or too imprecise to include in the official protocol proposal. RFC 57 offers them for discussion and possible inclusion in a second-level protocol.

The topics are error handling and overflow, and what hosts should do after going down and restarting.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors had ideas that were not ready for the official protocol. They documented them separately for discussion.

sections.title: Errors and Resource Overflow
sections.content:
The authors distinguish a real protocol error, such as an RFC with two send sockets, from overflow caused by exhausted system resources. Overflow does not mean someone made an error; the request can be repeated later.

Because RFC 54 reported overflow with CLS, a user could think a foreign process had refused the connection. The authors propose an OVF command that behaves like CLS while informing the user that the foreign host's resources were overtaxed. They also propose an 8-bit error-type field after the ERR opcode.
sections.plainLanguage: A malformed request and a full host are different problems. The authors propose different reporting so a user can tell whether to correct a request or try again later.

sections.title: Host Restart After a Crash
sections.content:
The memo distinguishes a soft crash, where the system has warning, from a hard crash with little warning and unpredictable state. After a hard crash, an NCP's data structures may be destroyed or meaningless.

The proposed RST command terminates connections with the sending host without sending CLS and announces that the sender is alive. A receiver responds with RSR, allowing hosts to update their live-host information. The authors note that handling old messages still in transit remains an open problem.
sections.plainLanguage: After a hard crash, hosts may need to discard old connection state and confirm which peers are alive. The proposed exchange does not solve the problem of messages already in transit.

sections.title: Proposed Error Types
sections.content:
The RFC lists error types numbered 0 through 9, from unspecified error to illegal socket specification for data. Other categories include illegal opcode, illegal command sequence, connection not open, and data overflow.

The list was developed while writing the pseudo-Algol program discussed in RFC 55.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed error field names the kind of problem, including invalid commands, connection state, or data size. This gives the recipient more specific information than a general error alone.

references.text: NWG/RFC 54, the official protocol proposal discussed in this memo.
Newkirk, J., Kraley, M., Postel, J., and S. Crocker, "A Prototypical Implementation of the NCP", RFC 55, June 1970.
